newsitem.title: UK: UK radio spectrum proceeds spread over decade.
newsitem.headline: UK radio spectrum proceeds spread over decade.

text.p: The one billion stg which the UK government may raise by auctioning the radio spectrum is likely to be spread over 10 years, a Department of Trade and Industry spokeswoman said on Thursday.

The Labour government has announced plans for a bill to ensure that fees paid by users of the airwaves reflect the economic value of the spectrum. Current licence fees are based merely on administrative costs.
The bill would not affect broadcasters, who already pay an economic rate under the terms of the Broadcasting Acts of 1990 and 1996.
It is aimed at business users such as taxi firms and mobile phone companies. But it will not affect existing long-term licence agreements which several mobile phone companies have signed.
The DTI spokeswoman noted that the plans to auction off the spectrum had been foreshadowed in draft legislation penned by the previous government last year.
Government officials have estimated that income from auctions could be in the order of one billion stg, but the spokeswoman said this would be spread over a decade.
Vodafone, which is the UK's largest mobile phone company with almost three million subscribers, stressed the auctions would apply only to new licences.
Its current licence was renewed just four years ago and has another 21 years to run.
"Our annual licence fee is currently around 1.5 million pounds and that will probably go up to 15 million by the end of the decade," said Terry Barwick, Vodafone director of corporate affairs.
"But that must be seen in the context of a company which made 1.4 billion turnover in the year to end-March 1996," he said.
Barwick said the increase in charges which Vodafone was budgeting for was to reflect higher administration charges. The DTI refused comment on this.
Vodafone dismissed suggestions that the changes would cost customers 10 pence per week.
Vodafone shares, which had shed 6.5p on Wednesday amid some confusion on the impact of the legislation, added 2.5p to 277.5p by 1440 GMT.
Rival Orange, which had also lost 6.5p on Wednesday, recouped 1p to 218p. An Orange spokeswoman pointed out that the company's licence rans until 2020.
"They will probably auction some new frequencies for the next generation of mobile phones but they are still in the development stage," said Vodafone's Barwick.

The DTI said that the use of radio contributes some 12 billion stg to GDP. It said further growth depends on the effective management of the spectrum and added that the current system led to inefficiencies and hoarding.
But it noted that higher charges would be limited to services and geographical areas where there is congestion. Around 80 percent of licensees are expected to pay no more than at present.
The Radiocommunications Agency, an executive arm of the DTI, manages most non-military spectrum in the UK and has income of 43 million stg from charges.
